body:
I think we should definitely move this stuff into IDL if possible. However, when I've tried in the past, I've gotten stuck. Basically, my intuition was that it would be too confusing to only move some of the stuff into IDL, and leave the rest in prose. Which means solving it all at once. Which is hard.

Some particular issues:

- Web IDL only allows identifiers (not strings) on the right-hand side of equals signs in extended attributes. So, we can't do `[Reflect="accept-charset"]` or even `[Reflect=accept-charset]`. We have to do something like `[Reflect=accept_charset]` with a heuristic that `_`s get converted to `-`s. This is silly. (But, we could probably fix it in Web IDL.)
- Should we require `[Reflect=bgcolor] attribute DOMString bgColor`, or can we assume lowercasing?
- How do we express clamped to a range? IDL syntax seems not flexible enough again.
- How do we express the various other numeric variants, i.e. limited to only non-negative numbers, limited to only non-negative numbers greater than zero, limited to only non-negative numbers greater than zero with fallback? Do they each get their own extended attribute? What do we name them that isn't ludicrously long?
- How do we handle enumerated attributes? You've provided some ideas above with ReflectEmpty/ReflectInvalid/ReflectMissing/ReflectOnly. But they don't map very well onto the spec's concepts, which are more like: is limited to only known values yes/no, missing value default state, invalid value default state, list of states, keyword -> state mapping. In particular the state -> keyword mapping is troubling. How do we handle cases like crossorigin="" where the missing value default state doesn't have a corresponding keyword at all? Maybe we should be using IDL enums, potentially one enum for keywords and one for states, but usually just one enum shared between both?? That'd be a big refactoring.

It's possible others would find it OK to only have some of the reflection defined in IDL and others defined in prose, at least for now. I'd welcome thoughts. But my instinct is to try to put in a lot of work to come up with the perfect scheme that covers all cases, including modifying Web IDL to give us better syntax, and do it all at once. Which is hard :).

If we have a rough plan for all of it, I wouldn't mind it landing in phases.

Some thoughts on the particulars:

* Implicit lowercasing seems fine.
* I also wouldn't mind potentially long names for the various numeric variants, though we could also make ReflectNumber accept a sequence of arguments.

cc @bzbarsky @tobie

> Web IDL only allows identifiers (not strings) on the right-hand side of equals signs in extended attributes. So, we can't do [Reflect="accept-charset"] or even [Reflect=accept-charset]. We have to do something like [Reflect=accept_charset] with a heuristic that _s get converted to -s. This is silly. (But, we could probably fix it in Web IDL.)

Quoting from [WebIDL](https://heycam.github.io/webidl/#idl-extended-attributes):

> The ExtendedAttribute grammar symbol matches nearly any sequence of tokens, however the extended attributes defined in this document only accept a more restricted syntax. Any extended attribute encountered in an IDL fragment is matched against the following five grammar symbols to determine which form (or forms) it is in: […]

So it's easy to add other forms, see for example the proposed wildcard attributed for `[Exposed]` in https://github.com/heycam/webidl/issues/468#issuecomment-340062144.

So adding support for `[Reflect="accept-charset"]` would be roughly trivial as adding the following non-terminal to the list of supported ExtendedAttribute grammar symbols:

```
ExtendedAttributeString :
    identifier "=" string
```
It should also be noted that at least Servo's, Gecko's and Blink's WebIDL parsers already understand this syntax.

Note that at least for `<canvas>`'s width/height there's also a requirement to be able to have some custom steps run before the reflecting steps. If the reflecting steps were all their own algorithms though that'd be fairly straightforward.

Edge also uses custom extended attributes for reflection. We've just added this for Edge15 (next version of Edge, so the syntax could change):

- [Reflect] Reflects the content attribute with the same name as the IDL attribute
- [Reflect="foo"] Reflects the content attribute named foo. We don't do implicit lowercasing so have Reflect="contenteditable" for example. I'd probably prefer implicit lowercasing to reduce characters/duplication
- [ReflectMissing=] Reflects missing value with value specified. keywords are quoted, numbers are not, e.g. ReflectMissing="auto" but ReflectMissing=0
- [ReflectInvalid=] Same as above for invalid values. Often set to empty string ReflectInvalid=""
- [ReflectValues=] List of valid values that are reflected. Range of values are in (), e.g. ReflectValues=("_blank"|"_self"|"_parent"|"_top"). A range of values of the same type is quoted, e.g. ReflectValues="bcp47_lang". Full list I can see: "bcp47_lang",  "mime_type", "character_encoding", "color", "font-family". The list of values in () can get fairly long however so might be nice if could define externally (especially if there are common shared value lists) like enums currently are.
- [ReflectType=""] Defines if values are space [ReflectType="space-separated"], or comma [ReflectType="comma-separated"] separated
-  [ReflectMinValue=number] The minimum value allowed, e.g. [Reflect="colspan", ReflectMinValue=1]

`[Foo=("_blank"|"_self"|"_parent"|"_top")]` is not a valid WebIDL syntax. Did you mean `,` instead of `|`?

https://heycam.github.io/webidl/#idl-extended-attributes
Seems like the only way to do that with current WebIDL is to do `(__blank, __self, __parent, __top)` (note the 2 underscores because the leading underscore in WebIDL identifiers should be stripped).
@nox, that's actually easy to fix, see: https://github.com/whatwg/html/issues/3238#issuecomment-345621963.
OTOH, `/_?[A-Za-z][0-9A-Z_a-z-]*/` doesn't even allow `__blank`.
CC @arronei
Re` [Foo=("_blank"|"_self"|"_parent"|"_top")]` That is just how we did it as it followed what we already had elsewhere in our code base. We`re happy to change it to commas.

Existing Content Attribute Reflection Extended Attributes
===============

## Blink Approach:

Blink makes use of a syntactic extension to the 5 limited syntaxes defined for ExtendedAttributes within the WebIDL specification. This is to allow strings to be used.

### [Reflect] and [Reflect=Identifier]

These can be used to indicate that an IDL attribute should reflect to a HTML content attribute, the optional Identifier indicates the name for the content attribute, this is used if they don't match (e.g. class and className).

### [ReflectOnly=string] and [ReflectOnly=(string,...)]

These are used alongside [Reflect] for when reflecting enumerated attributes that are limited to only known values. (e.g. popover attribute).

### [ReflectEmpty] and [ReflectEmpty=string]

These are used alongside [Reflect] and [ReflectOnly] and specifies the value when an enumerated attribute is present but empty. When no string is used it reflects to null for nullable IDL attributes and the empty string otherwise.

### [ReflectInvalid] and [ReflectInvalid=string]

These are used alongside [Reflect] and [ReflectOnly] and specifies the value when an enumerated attribute has an unknown value. When no string is used it reflects to null for nullable IDL attributes and the empty string otherwise.

### [RefectMissing] and [ReflectMissing=string]

These are used alongside [Reflect] and [ReflectOnly] and specifies the value when an enumerated attribute is missing. When no string is used it reflects to null for nullable IDL attributes and the empty string otherwise.

### [URL]

This is used alongside [Reflect] to indicate that a USVString represents a URL.


## WebKit Approach

### [Reflect] and [Reflect=Identifier]

These can be used to indicate that an IDL attribute should reflect to a HTML content attribute, the optional Identifier indicates the name for the content attribute, this is used if they don't match (e.g. class and className).

### [ReflectSetter] and [ReflectSetter=Identifier]

Like [Reflect] but only sets up reflection for the setter. This is useful in a number of cases where the setter is a simple "set the content attribute to the given value" but the getter is more complex.

### [URL]

This is used alongside [Reflect] to indicate that a USVString represents a URL.

### Enumerated attributes

WebKit has no IDL solution to these.


## Ladybird Approach

Ladybird makes use of a syntactic extension to the 5 limited syntaxes defined for ExtendedAttributes within the WebIDL specification. This is to allow values not represented by Identifiers to be used.

### [Reflect] and [Reflect=Identifier]

These can be used to indicate that an IDL attribute should reflect to a HTML content attribute, the optional Identifier indicates the name for the content attribute, this is used if they don't match (e.g. class and className).

### [Enumerated=Identifier]

This is used alongside [Reflect] for when reflecting enumerated attributes that are limited to only known values. The Identifier represents the Identifier for a WebIDL enum which is used to represent the enum of known values.

### [MissingValueDefault=SpecialIdentifier]

These are used on *the enum* identified by [Enumerated] and specifies the value when an enumerated attribute is missing.

### [InvalidValueDefault=SpecialIdentifier]

These are used on *the enum* identified by [Enumerated] and specifies the value when an enumerated attribute value is unknown.

### [URL]

This is used alongside [Reflect] to indicate that a USVString represents a URL.


## Gecko Approach

Gecko has no IDL handling for reflected attributes.

Though it should be noted Gecko *also* extends the ExtendedAttribute syntax range to allow for string values, this is used for at least [Pref].


## Servo Approach

Servo has no IDL handling for reflected attributes.


## JSDOM Approach

Based on Domenics comment here: https://github.com/whatwg/html/issues/3238#issuecomment-601383619

JSDOM makes use of syntactic extensions to the 5 limited syntaxes defined for ExtendedAttributes within the WebIDL specification.

This is to allow strings to be used for the ReflectX attributes. It's also to allow for numbers (I think Interger and Decimal tokens) within [ReflectRange=()] and [ReflectDefault=]

### [Reflect] and [Reflect=string]

These can be used to indicate that an IDL attribute should reflect to a HTML content attribute, the optional string indicates the name for the content attribute, this is used if they don't match (e.g. class and className).

### [ReflectURL] and [ReflectURL=string]

This is used *instead* of [Reflect] to indicate that a USVString IDL attribute should reflect and that the value represents a URL.

### [ReflectNonNegative] and [ReflectNonNegative=string]

This is used *instead* of [Reflect] to indicate that a long IDL attribute should reflect and that it's limited to only non-negative numbers.

### [ReflectPositive] and [ReflectPositive=string]

This is used *instead* of [Reflect] to indicate that an unsigned long IDL attribute should reflect and that it's limited to only positive numbers.

### [ReflectPositiveWithFallback] and [ReflectPositiveWithFallback=string]

This is used *instead* of [Reflect] to indicate that an unsigned long IDL attribute should reflect and that it's limited to only positive numbers with fallback.

### [ReflectPositiveWithFallback] and [ReflectPositiveWithFallback=string]

This is used *instead* of [Reflect] to indicate that an unsigned long IDL attribute should reflect and that it's limited to only positive numbers with fallback.

### [ReflectRange=(number, number)]

This is used *alongside* [Reflect] to indicate that an unsigned long IDL attribute should reflect and that it's clamped to the range [clampedMin, clampedMax].

### [ReflectDefault=number]

This is used *alongside* [Reflect] and, [ReflectNonNegative], [ReflectPositiveWithFallback], or [ReflectRange] to indicate the optional default value to be used.

### Enumerated attributes

JSDOM has no IDL solution to these.

# Proposed Standardised Reflection Extended Attributes

As can be seen there's no single approach that solves *all* use cases, nor do I think a specced solution would necessarily need to do that, some reflections are just too dynamic to declare and I think in those cases it's expected you'd still need spec prose. That being said I think a large chunk of defined spec reflection could be represented in IDL and handled by browser's (and JSDOMs) code generators.

Edited: I've updated this to account for Domenic and others feedback.

## Extended Attribute additional grammar

This proposal adds 3 new forms of grammar to that [defined by WebIDL](https://webidl.spec.whatwg.org/#idl-extended-attributes) (this isn't technically new syntax as WebIDL actually has very permissive parsing for ExtendedAttributes)

| Grammar Symbol | Form | Example |
| -------- | -------- | -------- |
| ExtendedAttributeString     | **takes a string**     | `[EmptyValue=""]`     |
| ExtendedAttributeNumber     | **takes an integer or decimal**     | `[ReflectDefault=2.0]`     |
| ExtendedAttributeIntegerList     | **takes a list of integers**     | `[ReflectRange=(5, 600)]`     |

ExtendedAttributeString ::
    **identifier** **=** **string**

ExtendedAttributeNumber ::
    **identifier** **=** **integer**
    **identifier** **=** **decimal**

ExtendedAttributeIntegerList ::
    **identifier** **=** **(** *IntegerList* **)**

IntegerList ::
    **integer** *Integers*

Integers ::
    **,** **integer** *Integers*
    **ε**


## [Reflect] and [Reflect=attributeName] (ExtendedAttributeNoArgs or ExtendedAttributeString)

These are valid on attribute interface members, when those attributes have a type `DOMString`, `DOMString?`, `USVString`, `boolean`, `long`, `unsigned long`, `double`, `DOMTokenList`, `T?`, or `FrozenArray<T>?`. Where `T` is a type of `Element`.

If an IDL attribute has [Reflect] then it's defined to reflect the content attribute with the same name.

If an IDL attribute has [Reflect=attributeName] then it's defined to reflect the content attribute *attributeName* (I'm sure we can find a nice spec prose for that)

## [ReflectURL] and [ReflectURL=attributeName] (ExtendedAttributeNoArgs or ExtendedAttributeString)

These are valid on attribute interface members, when those attributes have a type of `USVString`.

These behave the same as [Reflect] except additionally the content attribute indicates that it contains a URL. (This should probably be improved in the spec prose to as its ambiguous).

## [ReflectNonNegative] and [ReflectNonNegative=attributeName] (ExtendedAttributeNoArgs or ExtendedAttributeString)

These are valid on attribute interface members, when those attributes have a type of `long`.

These behave the same as [Reflect] except additionally it's [limited to only non-negative numbers](https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/common-dom-interfaces.html#limited-to-only-non-negative-numbers).

## [ReflectPositive] and [ReflectPositive=attributeName] (ExtendedAttributeNoArgs or ExtendedAttributeString)

These are valid on attribute interface members, when those attributes have a type of `double` and`unsigned long`.

These behave the same as [Reflect] except additionally it's [limited to only positive numbers](https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/common-dom-interfaces.html#limited-to-only-non-negative-numbers-greater-than-zero).

## [ReflectPositiveWithFallback] and [ReflectPositiveWithFallback=attributeName] (ExtendedAttributeNoArgs or ExtendedAttributeString)

These are valid on attribute interface members, when those attributes have a type of `unsigned long`.

These behave the same as [Reflect] except additionally it's [limited to only positive numbers with fallback](https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/common-dom-interfaces.html#limited-to-only-non-negative-numbers-greater-than-zero-with-fallback).

## [ReflectRange=(clampedMin, clampedMax)] (ExtendedAttributeIntegerList)

This is used alongside [Reflect] and augments how it works.

This is valid on attribute interface members, when those attributes have a type of `unsigned long`.

If an IDL attribute has [Reflect] and [ReflectRange] then it's [clamped to the range [clampedMin, clampedMax]](https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/common-dom-interfaces.html#clamped-to-the-range).

## [ReflectDefault=defaultValue] (ExtendedAttributeNumber)

This is used alongside [Reflect], [ReflectNegative], [ReflectPositive], or [ReflectPositiveWithFallback] and augments how they work.

This is valid on attribute interface members, when those attributes have a type of `double`, `long` or `unsigned long`.

If an IDL attribute has [Reflect] (etc) and [ReflectDefault] then it's [default value](https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/common-dom-interfaces.html#default-value) is defaultValue.

## [ReflectEnum=identifier] (ExtendedAttributeIdent)

This is used alongside [Reflect] and augment how it works.

These are valid on attribute interface members, when those attributes have a type of `DOMString` or `DOMString?`.

If an IDL attribute has [Reflect] and [ReflectEnum] then it's defined to reflect an enumerated content attribute (optionally identified by [Reflect=identifier]), [limited to only known values](https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/common-dom-interfaces.html#limited-to-only-known-values).

The identifier provided by [ReflectEnum] is the identifier of a WebIDL enum definition, this provides the list of known values e.g.

```webidl
interface ExampleElement {
    [Reflect, ReflectEnum=FooBarValues] attribute DOMString fooBar;
};

enum FooBarValues {
    "foo",
    "bar",
    "buz"
};
```

### [EmptyValueDefault] and [EmptyValueDefault=string]  (ExtendedAttributeNoArgs or ExtendedAttributeString)

These are valid on enumeration definitions.

If an IDL enum has [ReflectEmptyValue], and that enum is referenced by [ReflectEnum], then it augments the getter. When the value of the content attribute is the empty string, it will return the value defined by [ReflectEmptyValue], in the case that no string is provided it returns the empty string for `DOMString` and `null` for `DOMString?` attributes.

### [InvalidValueDefault] and [InvalidValueDefault=string]  (ExtendedAttributeNoArgs or ExtendedAttributeString)

These are valid on enumeration definitions.

If an IDL enum has [InvalidValueDefault], and that enum is referenced by [ReflectEnum], then it augments the getter.

This defines an [invalid value default](https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/common-microsyntaxes.html#invalid-value-default) state for the content attribute. Such that when the value of the content attribute is invalid, the getter will return the value defined by [InvalidValueDefault], in the case that no string is provided it returns the empty string for `DOMString` and `null` for `DOMString?` attributes.

### [MissingValueDefault] and [MissingValueDefault=string] (ExtendedAttributeNoArgs or ExtendedAttributeString)

These are valid on enumeration definitions.

This defines an [missing value default](https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/common-microsyntaxes.html#missing-value-default) state for the content attribute. Such that when the content attribute is missing, the getter will return the value defined by [MissingValueDefault], in the case that no string is provided it returns the empty string for `DOMString` and `null` for `DOMString?` attributes.

#### Possible syntax extension

If the WebIDL syntax were updated to allow ExtendedAttributeLists on Enum values then browsers would even be able to conditionally allow values based on runtime flags. This is a case where Chromium currently has to go back to a manual approach. e.g. on how you could represent an experimental hint addition to a stable popover attribute.

```webidl
interface HTMLElement {
    [Reflect, ReflectEnum=PopoverValues] attribute DOMString? popover;
};

[MissingValueDefault,InvalidValueDefault="manual",EmptyValueDefault="auto"]
enum PopoverValues {
    "auto",
    "manual",
    [RuntimeEnabled=PopoverHint]
    "hint"
};
```

## Possible Extras

While this covers most of the reflection there's some cases where it won't.

Type 1: Cases such as the HTMLElement.command property which has a straightforward setter but whose getter result depends on element state.

Type 2: Cases such as the HTMLElement.contentEditable property which has a straightforward getter but the setter is more complicated.

Type 3: Cases such as AriaMixin.ariaAtomic which [supports ElementInternals](https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/common-dom-interfaces.html#support-elementinternals).

Type 4: Other, I'm sure there's probably an example of some content attribute reflection that is just very complex and can't be declarative.

Type 1 could be addressed by a [ReflectSetter] extended attribute.

Type 2 could be addressed by a [ReflectGetter] extended attribute.

Type 3 could possibly be addressed by a [ReflectSupportsElementInternals] extended attribute (either replacing [Reflect] or augmenting it)

Type 4 should remain handled by spec prose.

Thanks for outlining this! I'd love to get something like this into the standard. As usual I'd suggest starting with non-enumerated attributes first since they're easier.

My comments are largely bikeshedding. I think the opinions of whoever actually signs up to do this work will have the most sway, but, maybe my bikeshedding comments are helpful anyway.

> `[Reflect=identifier]`

I prefer using strings for attribute names instead of identifiers, since that seems more faithful to the value space of attribute names.

> [ReflectNonNegative] This is used alongside [Reflect] and augment how it works.

I prefer the jsdom approach of using these _instead_ of `[Reflect]`, similar to how `[ReflectURL]` is used. The advantages are:

- It eliminates a potentially-invalid spec state, where you put `[ReflectNonNegative]` but don't put `[Reflect]` on an attribute.
- It's shorter.
- It matches `[ReflectURL]`.

The jsdom approach's philosophy is: there's always one primary attribute that causes reflection to happen, and its value, if it has one, is the attribute name. If reflection requires additional metadata, those go into other extended attributes.

> [ReflectEnum=identifier]

I generally like this approach. At first it appears a bit strange to have these `enum`s that aren't ever really used "as enums". But in the end, `enum`s are never reified anyway, even in "normal" usage: they exist only to help the bindings generator generate argument validation code. Having `enum`s that only exist to help the bindings generator generate reflection code is basically the same thing.

I'm less certain on how this will work in spec text, e.g., what you will do with the current enumerated attribute tables and definitions and informative summaries. But we'll see.

> As usual I'd suggest starting with non-enumerated attributes first since they're easier.

Yep I agree even adding just [Reflect] and [ReflectURL] would probably be a nice win. Though I thought I'd give it a go to outline everything, potentially we can do this in stages or in one go depending on what people think.

> I prefer using strings for attribute names instead of identifiers, since that seems more faithful to the value space of attribute names.

I was wondering about this. I don't think attribute names are ever invalid WebIDL identifiers? Their values are however. I think initially I was using "identitifier" to avoid new grammar but then we need it anyway. So yeah I would agree strings are probably better.

>> [ReflectNonNegative] This is used alongside [Reflect] and augment how it works.

> I prefer the jsdom approach of using these instead of [Reflect], similar to how [ReflectURL] is used. The advantages are:

> It eliminates a potentially-invalid spec state, where you put [ReflectNonNegative] but don't put [Reflect] on an attribute.

This would still be the case for [ReflectRange] and [ReflectDefaultValue] which both need to be augmentation.

> It's shorter.
> It matches [ReflectURL].

I was leaning towards simply making [ReflectURL] additional to [Reflect]. At least then it would all be consistent.

> The jsdom approach's philosophy is: there's always one primary attribute that causes reflection to happen, and its value, if it has one, is the attribute name. If reflection requires additional metadata, those go into other extended attributes.

I don't feel super strongly about this so if people prefer the JSDOM apparoach that's also fine. Though having [Reflect] be the canonical this triggers attribute reflection could be nice from an understanding point of view.

> I generally like this approach. At first it appears a bit strange to have these enums that aren't ever really used "as enums". But in the end, enums are never reified anyway, even in "normal" usage: they exist only to help the bindings generator generate argument validation code. Having enums that only exist to help the bindings generator generate reflection code is basically the same thing.

Yeah using enums was interesting at first but it solves needing even more new grammar to allow a list of strings in an extended attribute (or to do what I guess blink does which is use identifiers and then normalise the value to attribute value syntax in codegen), with extra WebIDL syntax (in the engine) you could do runtime enabled values which I think is quite a nice win, and yeah like you say ultimately IDL just serves to codegen anyway, this is just a slightly new usage of an enum for similar purposes to what it already does.

> I'm less certain on how this will work in spec text, e.g., what you will do with the current enumerated attribute tables and definitions and informative summaries. But we'll see.

Yeah that was where I was the most concerned about this approach but I think the same is true for any IDL approach to limited to known value attribute reflection.

Based on feedback I've update the proposal comment so [Reflect], [ReflectNegative], [ReflectPositive] and [ReflectPositiveWithFallback] are all mutually exclusive (and [ReflectURL] stays that way.

I've also swapped them to use ExtendedAttributeString rather than ExtendedAttributeIdent as Domenic mentioned.

For now [ReflectRange] is still a modifier for the other [Reflect] attributes, to allow both the Identifier and the NumberList you'd end up with quite complex grammar which would diminish the benefits imo.

I have a PR that adds the non enumerated attribute extended attributes.

Thinking on the enum case a bit more it's an interesting case. Because purely spec wise we just need something like `[ReflectKnown]` and `[ReflectKnown=string]` which triggers the [limited to only known values](https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/common-dom-interfaces.html#limited-to-only-known-values) case, because the *actual* definition is linked with the content attribute in the HTML spec prose.

The `[ReflectEnum=identifier]` along with `[MissingValueDefault]`, `[InvalidValueDefault]` and `[EmptyValueDefault]` are realistically purely *implementation* problems. Rather than spec ones.

So the question is what should we do here? Having a unified approach across browsers would be nice but does adding spec stuff purely for implementation reasons make sense?

I guess this is a question to the HTML editors? @domenic @annevk

> the _actual_ definition is linked with the content attribute in the HTML spec prose.

The whole point of this project is to get rid of the spec prose, and define all of this in IDL instead!

I think it'd be good to work through an example in more detail, like you started to do over Matrix. To my mind, the ideal outcome is that almost everything in

> The [popover](https://html.spec.whatwg.org/#attr-popover) attribute is an [enumerated attribute](https://html.spec.whatwg.org/#enumerated-attribute) with the following keywords and states:
>
> [... table ...]
>
> The attribute's [missing value default](https://html.spec.whatwg.org/#missing-value-default) is the No Popover state, and its [invalid value default](https://html.spec.whatwg.org/#invalid-value-default) is the [Manual](https://html.spec.whatwg.org/#attr-popover-manual-state) state.
>
> The popover IDL attribute must [reflect](https://html.spec.whatwg.org/#reflect) the [popover](https://html.spec.whatwg.org/#attr-popover) attribute, [limited to only known values](https://html.spec.whatwg.org/#limited-to-only-known-values).

gets replaced with IDL. Maybe the end result is something like

> The popover attribute is an enumerated attribute with the following enumerated values:
>
> [... table mapping enum values to prose brief descriptions ...]

and then all other parts of the spec start referring to enum values instead of to states. E.g. we'd define some new concept like "enumeration state" for a content attribute, which computes which enum value we're in depending on the current content attribute value.

I'm not sure if eliminating states in favor of enum values is totally possible. It might involve some awkward work. (Like for popover, some way of signaling that the empty string is not a state, even though it's a valid value for authors to use.) But I think this should be the end goal.

https://github.com/whatwg/html/commit/ce84350ec9640e686108bb1e47c3adc666eadfa0 covers everything except for enumerated attributes. And as you can see it has allowed us to remove quite a bit of prose.

https://github.com/whatwg/html/pull/11455 is the current draft by @lukewarlow for enumerated attributes.

(Removing agenda+ as we made a lot of progress here. If we want to keep it there someone should restate the goal of the discussion.)
See https://github.com/whatwg/html/issues/11516 for a follow-up discussion on the support ElementInternals flag to reflection.
